discovery: Programmable arrays of individually trapped neutral atoms entangled via the Rydberg blockade, for quantum simulation and computation

nominees.name: Antoine Browaeys
nominees.affiliation: Institut d'Optique Graduate School, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, France

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum information
motivation: In 2009 Browaeys (with Grangier) and Saffman independently showed the Rydberg blockade between two single atoms held in optical tweezers, and used it to entangle them. Lukin co-originated the theory of blockade-based gates and later led the scaling of the approach. Each atom is held and addressed individually, and the blockade gives a strong, switchable interaction between them. Together these turned isolated atoms into fully programmable quantum matter. Browaeys and Lukin assembled defect-free arrays of hundreds of atoms in any geometry. The arrays were used to observe quantum magnetism, topological spin liquids and quantum many-body scars. They also gave high-fidelity entangling gates and the first logical qubits with error detection in neutral atoms. This is the second quantum revolution in its purest form: entanglement and single-particle control, first explored in foundational experiments, have become a powerful tool for quantum simulation and computing.
